plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic array of circles arranged in six vertical columns, with arrows drawn among them and part of the field sitting on a gray background. Five columns hold five circles each, evenly stacked from top to bottom, while the rightmost column holds only three. In every full column the circle in the middle position is an open white disk and the remaining circles are filled solid black. The white disk in the third column from the left carries the italic label x. Straight vertical arrows within each full column run upward from lower circles to the middle disk and from that disk to the circle above, and long curved arrows arc from a column's bottom circle to its topmost one. Along the row of white disks, horizontal arrows point inward toward x: the disks in the fourth through sixth columns send arrows leftward into x, with farther ones curving above intervening columns, and x in turn sends arrows leftward to the disks in the second and first columns. A rounded gray region with stepped edges covers the two circles below x in its own column together with the white disk and every circle beneath it in each column to the right. Because each arrow encodes an ordering between two elements, the shaded block gathers the elements the arrow chains place on one side of x, turning a counting argument about the quality of a partition into a visible area.

elements: six vertical columns of circles (columns 1-5 with five circles each, column 6 with three circles)
open white disks at the middle (third) row of every column, black outline
solid black filled circles at all non-middle positions
italic label 'x' placed just below-right of the white disk in column 3 (the median of medians)
short vertical arrows inside each full column: from the bottom black circle up to the white disk, and from the white disk up to the circle above it
long curved arrows arcing from each full column's bottom-most circle up to its top-most circle (columns 1-5)

horizontal arrows along the white-disk row pointing inward toward x: columns 4, 5, 6 send leftward arrows into x (farther ones curving above the intervening columns), and x sends leftward arrows to the white disks of columns 2 and 1
rounded gray shaded region with stepped edges covering the two circles below x in column 3 plus the white disk and every circle beneath it in columns 4, 5, 6 (the 'known greater than x' block)
mirror rounded gray region (for the toggle) covering the two circles above x in column 3 plus the white disk and every circle above/beside it in columns 1, 2 (the 'known less than x' block)
highlight overlay color applied to x, its certified arrow chains, and the affected circles when x is clicked

interactions.label: Proof phase
interactions.teaches: Each press adds exactly one visual layer of the SELECT counting argument: first the n elements are seen as columns of five, then each column's median (white disk) is identified, then the median-of-medians x is chosen, and finally the elements provably on one side of x are gathered into a shaded area — making the 3n/10 lower bound a visible region rather than an algebraic step.

Clicking x brightens every arrow chain that certifies a comparison to the median-of-medians: the vertical within-group orderings plus the horizontal median-to-median orderings. The learner sees that an element in the shaded block is known to exceed x by transitivity (group-median >= x, then element >= its group-median), so it can be counted without ever being directly compared to x.

interactions.label: Certified region
interactions.teaches: Switching sides moves the shaded block from the columns whose median is >= x (right of and below x) to the columns whose median is <= x (left of and above x), exposing the symmetric partition guarantee: at least 3n/10 - 6 elements lie on EACH side of x, which is what bounds the recursive call.

demo_steps.title: 1. Group into fives
demo_steps.narration: The n input elements are drawn as vertical columns of five (the last column may be short). No ordering is assumed yet — this is just the grouping step of SELECT.

demo_steps.title: 2. Mark group medians
demo_steps.narration: Within each column the elements are sorted and the middle one is opened up as a white disk; the vertical arrows record the within-group order. These white disks are the group medians.

demo_steps.title: 3. Choose the median of medians x
demo_steps.narration: The median of the white disks is selected and labeled x (column 3). Horizontal arrows now point toward x from every other group median, encoding which medians are >= x and which are <= x.

demo_steps.title: 4. Shade elements known greater than x
demo_steps.narration: The gray block gathers, in every column whose median is >= x, that median and the two elements above-certified within the group, plus the two elements below x in its own column. Counting these cells gives the >= 3n/10 - 6 guarantee.

demo_steps.title: 5. Flip to the symmetric side
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to 'Known less than x': the shaded block mirrors to the left/upper side. The same counting applies, confirming x is a balanced pivot and the recursion shrinks to at most 7n/10 + 6 elements.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Pure 2D front-on schematic (axis_screen_angles null). Lay out a 6-column grid: column centers at X = -5, -3, -1, +1, +3, +5 (spacing 2); row centers at Y = +4, +2, 0, -2, -4 (spacing 2). Circle radius ~0.38 world units. White disks (white fill #ffffff, black stroke #000000, stroke ~0.06) sit at row Y=0 in all six columns; all other present cells are solid black #000000 disks. Column 6 contains only rows Y=+2, 0, -2. The italic 'x' label sits at about (X=-0.55, Y=-0.55) beside the column-3 white disk. Short vertical arrows (black, with triangular heads) connect Y=-2->0 and 0->+2 within each full column; long curved arrows (quadratic bezier bulging left) connect Y=-4 -> +4 in columns 1-5. Horizontal arrows run along Y=0: from columns 4,5,6 white disks leftward into x (columns 5,6 arcing above via a bezier raised to ~Y=+1.2), and from x leftward to columns 2,1 white disks. Gray region (greater) is a rounded rect roughly X in [-2.0, +6.0], Y in [-4.6, +0.6] with a stepped notch excluding column-3's upper cells; color #b3b3b3 at ~0.55 opacity, drawn BEHIND circles. The 'less' region mirrors to X in [-6.0, +0.0], Y in [-0.6, +4.6]. Highlight color for click = orange #ff7a00 applied to x, its certified arrows, and certified circles. Counting check: greater block = 3 columns (4,5,6) x 3 cells + 2 cells below x = 11 cells shown, illustrating the >= 3*floor(n/5)/2 - ... ~ 3n/10 - 6 bound.
interactionPlan.notes: Render with an orthographic-style front camera (no perspective depth). Circles as THREE.CircleGeometry meshes (white disks get an additional ring/LineLoop for the outline). Arrows as THREE.Line with QuadraticBezierCurve3 sampling for the curved ones, plus small cone/triangle arrowheads oriented along the tangent. The gray region as a rounded-rect THREE.Shape (ShapeGeometry) with a stepped inner cut, placed at a slightly negative z so circles and arrows draw on top. Phase button controls visibility groups: phase>=1 shows columns; phase>=2 opens white disks + vertical arrows; phase>=3 adds label x + horizontal arrows; phase>=4 adds the gray region (side chosen by the toggle). Click on x toggles an emissive/color boost on the certified subgraph; recompute the certified set from the arrow adjacency so the highlight exactly matches the transitive chains. Keep all geometry static per phase and only toggle visibility/opacity for smooth transitions.

authoredContext: We now examine a selection algorithm whose running time is O.n/ in the worst case. Like RANDOMIZED-SELECT, the algorithm SELECT finds the desired element by recursively partitioning the input array. Here, however, we guarantee a good split upon partitioning the array. SELECT uses the deterministic partitioning algorithm PARTITION from quicksort (see Section 7.1), but modified to take the element to partition around as an input parameter. The SELECT algorithm determines the ith smallest of an input array of n > 1 distinct elements by executing the following steps. (If n D 1, then SELECT merely returns its only input value as the ith smallest.) 1. Divide the n elements of the input array into bn=5c groups of 5 elements each and at most one group made up of the remaining n mod 5 elements. 2. Find the median of each of the dn=5e groups by first insertion-sorting the elements of each group (of which there are at most 5) and then picking the median from the sorted list of group elements. 3. Use SELECT recursively to find the median x of the dn=5e medians found in step 2. (If there are an even number of medians, then by our convention, x is the lower median.) 4. Partition the input array around the median-of-medians x using the modified version of PARTITION. Let k be one more than the number of elements on the low side of the partition, so that x is the kth smallest element and there are nk elements on the high side of the partition. 5. If i D k, then return x. Otherwise, use SELECT recursively to find the ith smallest element on the low side if i < k, or the .i k/th smallest element on the high side if i > k. To analyze the running time of SELECT, we first determine a lower bound on the number of elements that are greater than the partitioning element x. Figure 9.1 helps us to visualize this bookkeeping.

Along the row of white disks, horizontal arrows point inward toward x: the disks in the fourth through sixth columns send arrows leftward into x, with farther ones curving above intervening columns, and x in turn sends arrows leftward to the disks in the second and first columns. A rounded gray region with stepped edges covers the two circles below x in its own column together with the white disk and every circle beneath it in each column to the right. Because each arrow encodes an ordering between two elements, the shaded block gathers the elements the arrow chains place on one side of x, turning a counting argument about the quality of a partition into a visible area.
